newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips profit slump triggers S&P warning.
newsitem.headline: Philips profit slump triggers S&P warning.

text.p: Philips Electronics, grappling with falling prices and flagging markets, stunned investors on Thursday with a 77 percent slump in third quarter profit and also drew a warning from rating agency S&P.

Europe's biggest consumer electronics company reported a drop in net profit from normal operations to 123 million guilders ($72 million) from 539 million a year ago -- half the the 240-360 million guilder range that analysts had forecast.
New chairman Cor Boonstra said Philips would tackle its problems head-on through a company-wide reorganisation and issued targets for recovery.
Boonstra told reporters that Philips was looking for double digit growth in 1997 income from operations and targeted a big rise in return on net operating capital.

"I will also take head-on what I call the bleeders in the company, that means we will turn around, sell or close businesses that are not performing to our standards or are not fitting into our portfolio."

Philips said it would include a one billion guilder one-off charge for restructuring in its current fourth quarter, coming on top of an 800 million guilder gross charge for a similar exercise it announced for its Sound & Vision unit in July.
Analysts were encouraged by the tough talk from Boonstra, who took over from Jan Timmer on October 1.

ING Barings analyst Eric de Graaf said he had been braced for a big third-quarter profit fall, but was encouraged that Boonstra was clearly identifying problems and setting out a strategy to deal with them.
"Boonstra has stated unambiguously that if activities are not performing well they will be sold or closed down... I am very positive about that," he said.

But rating agency Standard & Poor's was less charitable, revising its outlook on Philips' long-term debt issues to negative from stable, and saying it might be forced to review its triple-B plus senior debt and corporate credit rating.

"The outlook change reflects the company's disappointing financial performance for the nine months ended September 1996... If management's objectives of restoring profitability and cash flow generation during 1997 are not met, Standard & Poor's may lower its ratings on the company," it said.
Philips, which had already targeted a net 6,000 job cuts at its Sound & Vision unit, said more jobs would go in the next restructuring, but refused to be drawn on specifics.
"There will be a loss of jobs in those areas which are high cost and a gaining of jobs in those geographical areas which offer lower cost labour," finance director Dudley Eustace said.
"It's a fair guess to say more jobs will be lost than gained in western Europe," he said, adding: "I would hope that the bulk of these measures will have been completed by the end of next year."
Eustace highlighted the performance in Asia where nine month operating profit rose, but said Europe and North America suffered heavily from price erosion and slack markets.

"The story is a sad one for Europe and North America where price pressures are at their strongest and demand at its weakest. The solution can only come from increased pressure on costs which ultimately leads to fewer jobs."

Boonstra said Philips was targeting sustainable double-digit growth in income from operations during the course of 1997. Return on net assets should rise to 24 percent next year from a current 8.4 percent, he said.
But he fought shy of giving investors and markets a clearer idea of Philips' corporate strategy.
"When the roof is leaking, fix it before you buy a new kitchen. I will come back to you on the subject of corporate strategy, we're looking at it, but first things first."

He took pains to point out that Philips was not in the same position as it was in the early 1990s when Timmer brought in the Centurion recovery progamme, hauling the firm back from the brink of disaster after big losses.
"The company six years ago was in a state of danger of bankruptcy. That is not the case today. We are in a financically much better position," he said.
Ad van der Laar of Bank Labouchere was sceptical on Boonstra's performance targets, although he stressed he was awaiting further details from a corporate briefing for analysts.
"They (the targets) are very ambitious, to say the least," Van der Laar said. "But what else can Boonstra say?"

Philips shares plunged on first reading of the third quarter figures, dropping 3.60 guilders, or more than five percent, to 53.00. But they rallied on Boonstra's comments to stand 2.50 guilders higher at 59.10 guilders by mid-afternoon in Amsterdam.
